lead.text: Attacker-controlled JSON request bodies are written unsanitized to the process log in the JAX-RS demo handlers, allowing log forging/injection. ArrayResource.doPost (an :EntryPoint, exposure='reachable') receives a parsed JsonStructure from the HTTP request body and passes it straight to System.out.println(structure) at ArrayResource.java:42. The same pattern appears at ObjectResource.java:53 and StructureResource.java:52. Because JsonStructure.toString() reproduces attacker-supplied string contents, an attacker who embeds newline/CR characters in JSON string values can inject forged log records. Note this is reached via the structure's toString(), not via JsonGeneratorImpl's escaping path, so the generator's control-character escaping does not apply. These are demo modules rather than the shipped impl/ library, which caps real-world impact.

reason: The sink and its reachability are real, but the vulnerability MECHANISM the lead depends on is contradicted by the source. The lead's load-bearing assertion -- "this is reached via the structure's toString(), not via JsonGeneratorImpl's escaping path, so the generator's control-character escaping does not apply" -- is exactly inverted. The structure's toString() IS the generator escaping path. Traced: JsonParserImpl.getObject() builds the parsed body via JsonObjectBuilderImpl (JsonParserImpl.java:152), whose build() yields JsonObjectImpl (JsonObjectBuilderImpl.java:217); JsonObjectImpl.toString() (JsonObjectBuilderImpl.java:327-333) creates a JsonWriterImpl and calls jw.write(this); JsonWriterImpl is "JsonWriter impl using generator" (JsonWriterImpl.java:29) holding a JsonGeneratorImpl (line 35); and JsonGeneratorImpl.writeEscapedString() (lines 541-591) passes through only chars matching `c >= 0x20 && c <= 0x10ffff && c != 0x22 && c != 0x5c`, routing EVERY char below 0x20 into the escape switch (\n -> \\n, \r -> \\r, default -> \uXXXX). Object keys are escaped on the same path via writeName -> writeEscapedString (line 149). Arrays take the identical route (JsonArrayImpl.toString(), JsonArrayBuilderImpl.java:472-478). Independently, JsonStringImpl.toString() (JsonStringImpl.java:67-106) re-implements the same control-character escaping. Consequently an attacker-supplied value such as {"a":"x\ny"} is parsed into a raw 0x0A in memory but re-encoded by toString() into the two literal characters backslash+n, so no raw CR/LF can ever reach the log record; newline-based log forging is not achievable on this path. (A literal unescaped newline inside a JSON string in the request body is a parse error per RFC 8259 anyway.) The sanitizer the lead claims is bypassed sits directly on the path, twice over. Skipped exploit_search as not applicable: this is a code-pattern claim about Parsson's own source, not a versioned-dependency CVE, and it fails on mechanism rather than version.

lead.text: An attacker-inflated tokenizer buffer is retained indefinitely in a shared, uncapped buffer pool, turning a transient spike into persistent memory retention. After fillBuf() has doubled `buf` to an attacker-chosen size, JsonTokenizer.close() hands that oversized array to the shared pool via `jsonContext.bufferPool().recycle(buf)` (JsonTokenizer.java:583). BufferPoolImpl.recycle() is simply `getQueue().offer(t)` -- it performs no size cap on the queue and no check that the returned array is the standard 4096-char size it hands out in take(). Because the default pool is shared across parsers/requests, multi-megabyte buffers from hostile documents accumulate in the ConcurrentLinkedQueue and are only reclaimable when the WeakReference wrapping the whole queue is cleared, so memory is not released after the offending request completes. fillBuf() at line 478 likewise recycles the pre-doubling buffer on every growth step, offering progressively larger arrays into the same unbounded queue.

reason:
All of the lead's structural premises are real and I confirmed each at the exact cited line, but its security conclusion -- indefinite/persistent memory retention, CWE-401 -- does not follow, so the finding is a false positive.

VERIFIED TRUE: BufferPoolImpl.recycle() is a bare `getQueue().offer(t)` with no queue-length cap and no element-size validation (BufferPoolImpl.java:69-72); take() hands out `new char[4096]` (lines 44-49); JsonTokenizer.close() recycles `buf` at line 583 and fillBuf() doubles `buf` then recycles the pre-growth array at lines 477-479 (both exactly as claimed); `buf` originates from the pool (JsonTokenizer.java:125); the pool is one shared instance (`private final BufferPool bufferPool = new BufferPoolImpl()`, JsonProviderImpl.java:44) used by every JsonContext; there is no max-string-length limit (JsonContext caps only BigDecimal length=1100, BigInteger scale, depth=1000); and the graph confirms recycle is reachable (reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=4). Reachability is therefore NOT the reason for rejection.

WHY IT IS STILL NOT A VULNERABILITY: I grepped `queue|WeakReference` across all of impl/src/main/java and the identifier occurs ONLY inside BufferPoolImpl.java. The single long-lived reference to the ConcurrentLinkedQueue is the `WeakReference` field at line 32; getQueue() returns a transient local `d` that take()/recycle() use only within the call. Hence, between pool operations, the queue AND every char[] it contains are merely WEAKLY REACHABLE. Two consequences kill the claim: (1) any GC cycle may clear the reference and reclaim the entire queue plus all pooled buffers -- that is the normal steady state, not the remote contingency the lead implies; (2) the JVM is required to clear weak references to weakly-reachable objects and reclaim them BEFORE throwing OutOfMemoryError, so pooled buffers can never drive heap exhaustion -- under exactly the memory pressure an attacker would need, the pool is discarded first. The lead's assertions that the buffers are "retained indefinitely" and that "memory is not released after the offending request completes" are therefore false. The WeakReference is deliberate design that prevents unbounded pooled retention; the analyst identified it but inverted its significance, treating the always-active reclamation path as an unlikely escape hatch.

RESIDUAL (not the claimed defect, and not used to rescue it): one hostile document does transiently leave the whole doubling sequence plus the final buffer (~2N chars) in the pool, but only until the next GC -- bounded and self-releasing, not a leak. The genuine attack surface here is the unbounded doubling of `buf` itself in fillBuf to hold an arbitrarily long string (CWE-789, no max-string-length option in this version), which is a different defect at a different location whose buffer is reclaimed normally once the parser is dereferenced.

lead.text: The MAX_BIGDECIMAL_LEN mitigation is enforced too late to prevent the memory cost it was added to stop. JsonTokenizer.getBigDecimal() rejects oversized numeric literals at line 521 (`sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()` -> UnsupportedOperationException, default 1100 chars), but that check runs only at BigDecimal *conversion* time. By then readNumber()/readNumberChar() -> read() -> fillBuf() have already buffered the entire numeric token and grown `buf` by unbounded doubling (line 477). So a JSON document containing one gigantic numeric literal (e.g. a 500MB run of digits) exhausts memory during tokenization and never reaches the length check -- and if the parser is driven with nextToken()/getString() rather than getBigDecimal(), the check is never consulted at all. The limit guards only the `new BigDecimal(buf, storeBegin, sourceLen)` CPU cost, not the buffering allocation.

reason:
The cited code all exists exactly as described, but the security conclusion is wrong on three counts I verified in source.

(1) The "unbounded doubling" is bounded by input size. fillBuf() gates growth on `storeLen == buf.length` (JsonTokenizer.java:475) -- the retained token must already fill the ENTIRE buffer before Arrays.copyOf doubles it. Therefore buf.length <= 2 x tokenLen <= 2 x inputLen at all times. There is NO amplification: the lead's "500MB run of digits" requires the attacker to actually transmit 500MB to cost ~1GB heap (2 bytes/char, transient 3x during copyOf). Memory proportional to the request body is the caller's/container's request-size-limit responsibility, not a parser defect. Critically, a SMALL input cannot trigger large buffering -- e.g. `1E+2147483647` yields a short token -- so the amplifying cases are exactly the ones the limits do guard.

(2) The limit is placed precisely where the cost it guards lives, not "too late". JsonContext.java:40 documents it as "maximum number of characters of BigDecimal source being parsed", and JsonBigDecimalLengthLimitTest.java:60-71 asserts a 501-char literal throws -- the intent is bounding the SUPER-LINEAR `new BigDecimal(char[],off,len)` digit->binary conversion, and the check sits immediately before that call at line 527. Its companion bigIntegerScaleLimit (JsonNumberImpl.java:290-308) bounds the toBigInteger expansion. Both genuinely amplifying paths (tiny input -> huge cost) are guarded. The lead re-attributes the mitigation to a purpose it never had (bounding tokenizer buffering) and then faults it for not serving that purpose.

(3) The getString() "bypass" incurs no super-linear cost. JsonParserImpl.java:84-87 routes VALUE_NUMBER to tokenizer.getValue() (JsonTokenizer.java:509-511), a single linear `new String(buf, storeBegin, storeEnd-storeBegin)` copy. Skipping getBigDecimal() means never incurring the cost the limit exists to bound -- correct behavior, not an evasion.

Nothing here is numeric-specific: readString() (JsonTokenizer.java:128-156) uses the identical read()/fillBuf() doubling with NO length limit whatsoever, and object-model construction amplifies far worse (`[1,1,1,...]` -> one JsonNumberImpl per 2 input bytes, ~20x). lead.text: BOM magic-byte detection in UnicodeDetectingInputStream.detectEncoding() is gated on `bufLen == 4`, so every BOM literal pattern (NUL/FE/FF/EF/BB/BF) is only ever compared when exactly 4 bytes were buffered. Inputs that buffer 2 or 3 bytes fall straight through to `return StandardCharsets.UTF_8` with curIndex left at 0, meaning the BOM bytes are never consumed and are handed to the JSON tokenizer as content. A 3-byte UTF-8-BOM-only document (EF BB BF) and a 2-byte UTF-16 BOM (FE FF / FF FE) both mis-detect: the UTF-16 cases are silently decoded as UTF-8. The correct gate is `bufLen >= 2` with per-prefix length checks, not an exact-4 equality.

WHY IT IS NOT EXPLOITABLE: fillBuf() (L58-101) uses single-byte blocking `in.read()`, which returns -1 only at true EOF, so bufLen<4 implies the whole document is under 4 bytes -- there is no short-read window that could starve a large BOM'd document. Any BOM plus even one character of content is already >=4 bytes (UTF-8 3+1, UTF-16 2+2, UTF-32 4), so all real BOM'd documents take the correct branch; the existing test JsonParserTest.java:112 ("[]".getBytes(UTF_16) => FE FF 00 5B 00 5D) passes through L115 and is correctly detected as UTF-16BE. Both paths reject with a JsonParsingException, so no input produces a successful-but-different parse. Note specifically that 4.13.2 is NOT affected by CVE-2020-15250 (the TemporaryFolder information-disclosure issue), which was fixed in 4.13.1 — so the lead here is EOL/unmaintained status, not that known CVE; a verifier should not promote this to a CVE hit on version alone.

reason: The version fact is real but carries no security impact, so it is not a vulnerability. Verified myself: (1) junit 4.13.2 IS pinned at pom.xml:424-428 and matches the :Dependency graph node — the analyst did not fabricate it. (2) However it is TEST-SCOPE ONLY: both real consuming declarations use <scope>test</scope> (impl/pom.xml:99-103, demos/customprovider-jdk9/pom.xml:76-80), and demos isn't even in the root <modules> list (only impl, rest, bundles). (3) ZERO production usage — all 23 files importing org.junit are under src/test/java; no main-source import exists anywhere in the tree. (4) NOT SHIPPED — the dist assembly (bundles/dist/src/main/assembly/archive.xml:35-58) uses an explicit allow-list of only jakarta.json-api, parsson, org.eclipse.parsson:jakarta.json and parsson-media, so junit cannot reach any distributable; the OSGi bundle (bundles/jakarta.json/pom.xml:169) does not embed it. (5) NO GRAPH FOOTPRINT — a Cypher query for any CpgMethod whose full_name or file_path contains 'junit' returned 0 rows, so there is no sink, no reachable path and no attack-surface node. (6) NO VULNERABLE RANGE — 4.13.2 is the terminal, fully-patched JUnit 4 release; CVE-2020-15250 was fixed in 4.13.1, which the analyst correctly conceded, so there is no unpatched defect to match. The exploit corpus was unavailable ('not indexed'), but no exploit claim was made and none is needed. What remains is solely 'JUnit 4 is an EOL major line'. CWE-1104 requires the unmaintained component to form part of the product's attack surface; here it is a build-time test harness, pinned to the final patched release of its line, never loaded at runtime, absent from every distributable and absent from the call graph. No input, no state and no attacker-reachable path exist, so no failure scenario can be constructed — this is dependency hygiene / tech debt for the test suite, not a security finding.

lead.text: Declared dependency `jakarta.servlet-api` is pinned to 5.0.0 (Jakarta EE 9, 2020) while the current line is 6.x — an outdated API component. The repo does consume the servlet API in first-party code (demos/servlet/ArrayServlet.java and providers/*/TestServlet.java are in the file set, and `req.getQueryString()` appears as a real call there), so this is a live compile/runtime dependency rather than an unused declaration.

reason: The lead's structural facts are real but carry no security weight, so it is a false positive. (1) jakarta.servlet-api is a pure API/specification artifact (interfaces, abstract classes, annotations) with no server implementation — servlet-layer vulnerabilities live in the container (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow) that supplies the implementation, not in the spec stub. (2) Both consumers declare it <scope>provided</scope> (demos/servlet/pom.xml:32, providers/pom.xml:37), so it is compile-classpath only, is never bundled into any distributable, and "5.0.0" is not the code that executes at runtime. (3) The pin is confined to demo/test modules: it lives in a profile <dependencyManagement> explicitly commented "dependencies used by demo projects only" (pom.xml:451) governing the providers/demos modules (pom.xml:466-469), while the actually shipped library impl/parsson depends only on jakarta.json-api (impl/pom.xml:97) and junit — no servlet-api — so no downstream Parsson consumer ever receives this dependency. (4) The analyst's "corroborating" taint flow is benign: the only use of req.getQueryString() is q.equals("stream") at ArrayServlet.java:56, a comparison against a string literal that selects between two JsonWriter constructors; the value is never reflected, concatenated, or passed to any parser/command/query, and the JSON emitted is hardcoded (lines 43-50). Both TestServlets ignore req entirely, and a repo-wide grep shows getQueryString is the ONLY request-data read anywhere (no getParameter/getHeader). Finally, version currency is not a weakness: Servlet 5.0->6.0 is a Jakarta EE 9->10 platform baseline bump (Java 11->17), not a security fix, and CWE-1104 requires an UNMAINTAINED component, whereas the Jakarta Servlet spec is actively maintained and 5.0.0 is a released, supported spec level. lead.text: Software-composition blind spot: 6 of the 11 declared Dependency nodes carry an unresolved Maven property placeholder as their version string instead of a concrete version — jakarta.annotation-api (${jakarta.annotation-api.version}), jakarta.json (${project.version}), jakarta.json-api (${jakarta.json-api.version}), jakarta.ws.rs-api (${jakarta.ws.rs-api.version}), jakarta.xml.bind-api (${jakarta.xml.bind-api.version}), parsson-media (${project.version}). Any version-matching SCA pass over this manifest cannot evaluate those six components at all, so a known-vulnerable version among them would be silently missed. The verifier should resolve the effective versions from the parent pom's <properties> block / dependencyManagement before concluding the dependency set is clean.
lead.evidence:
Query: MATCH (d:Dependency {scan_id:$scan_id}) RETURN d.name AS name, d.version AS version ORDER BY name
Result (11 rows total): hamcrest-core=1.3, jakarta.annotation-api=${jakarta.annotation-api.version}, jakarta.json=${project.version}, jakarta.json-api=${jakarta.json-api.version}, jakarta.servlet-api=5.0.0, jakarta.ws.rs-api=${jakarta.ws.rs-api.version}, jakarta.xml.bind-api=${jakarta.xml.bind-api.version}, jaxb-impl=3.0.1, junit=4.13.2, parsson=${project.version}, parsson-media=${project.version} — i.e. exactly 6 unresolved ${...} placeholders and 5 concrete versions.

reason:
The underlying graph data is accurate (I reproduced the query and got the identical 11 rows with 6 placeholder versions), but it is not a vulnerability — it is an artifact of the scanner's manifest extractor reading raw XML without Maven property interpolation.

(1) Every placeholder resolves within the SAME file, pom.xml, with no external parent required: jakarta.json-api.version=2.1.2 (line 99), jakarta.annotation-api.version=2.1.1 (line 101), jakarta.xml.bind-api.version=4.0.0 (line 102), jakarta.ws.rs-api.version=3.1.0 (line 103), and ${project.version}=1.1.3-SNAPSHOT (line 33). The consuming <dependencyManagement> is at lines 387-436 of that same file. The external parent org.eclipse.ee4j:project:1.0.8 is not needed for any of the six.

(2) Three of the six are NOT third-party components: org.eclipse.parsson:jakarta.json (defined at bundles/jakarta.json/pom.xml:30-31), org.eclipse.parsson:parsson-media (rest/pom.xml:30-31), and org.eclipse.parsson:parsson are first-party modules built from this very repository, carrying ${project.version} by design to version-lock to the reactor. No advisory feed exists to match them against.

(3) The lead's falsifiable prediction ("a known-vulnerable version among them would be silently missed") is disproved by performing the resolution the lead itself requested. The four genuine third-party artifacts resolve to jakarta.annotation-api 2.1.1, jakarta.json-api 2.1.2, jakarta.ws.rs-api 3.1.0, jakarta.xml.bind-api 4.0.0 — all API/specification jars (interfaces and annotations, effectively no executable logic) at current versions for their spec generation, none known-vulnerable. The concrete-versioned remainder is clean too: junit 4.13.2 is itself the fix for CVE-2020-15250; jakarta.servlet-api 5.0.0 and jaxb-impl 3.0.1 are demo/provided scope.

(4) Centralizing versions via ${property} with <properties> + <dependencyManagement> is Maven's documented best practice, not a defect. CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components) requires identifying an actually unmaintained or vulnerable component; the lead identifies none and none exists here.

Note: exploit_search returned "corpus unavailable: not indexed", so the advisory exploit cross-check could not run. It was not load-bearing, since no component resolved to a version requiring one.
